corrections.caveats: Wrapper of Skia (google/skia is already listed): Rust napi-rs glue plus a C/C++ Skia shim (skia-c) exposing a JavaScript/TypeScript API for Node.js only, not callable from C++. The gain is Skia's CPU raster backend versus Cairo, so the entry is evidence that Skia beats Cairo rather than a new rasterizer. The cross-library table was run by the skia-canvas author (a competitor, so independent of this project) as a single run on one MacBook Air M3 (data.json reports 330 MiB free memory), with prebuilt npm binaries whose compiler and flags are unknown. Every timed iteration includes PNG or JPEG encoding with each library's own encoder settings, so rows mix raster and encode time and output sizes differ. Several rows are at parity: get/put ImageData 283 ms vs 272 ms (slightly slower), SVG to SVG and SVG to PDF 1.0x (both node-canvas and @napi-rs/canvas embed the SVG as a bitmap), PDF to PNG 1.1x, text 1.2x. corrections.caveats: Wrapper of Skia (google/skia is already listed): Rust (Neon) glue over rust-skia with a JavaScript API for Node.js only, not callable from C++; the gain over Cairo is Skia's, so the entry is evidence that Skia beats Cairo rather than a new rasterizer. First-party: the benchmark repo and results are by the skia-canvas author, a single run on one laptop. GPU versus CPU: skia-canvas renders bitmaps on the GPU by default (Metal on macOS, 4x MSAA by default; docs/api/canvas.md and CHANGELOG.md), and the harness creates `new Canvas(w, h)` without `gpu:false` except in the get/put ImageData test (tests/image-rw.js sets `canvas.gpu = false`), so the serial and async drawing rows very likely ran on the M3 GPU while node-canvas used Cairo's CPU rasterizer and @napi-rs/canvas Skia's CPU raster backend; the engine actually used was not logged. The async rows start every iteration at once in Promise.all on skia-canvas's native worker pool while the baseline renders one at a time, so they measure parallelism; the serial rows are the fairer comparison. In SVG to SVG and SVG to PDF the canvas and @napi-rs/canvas baselines embed the SVG as a bitmap while skia-canvas writes vectors, so those rows are not the same work. Each iteration includes encoding with different settings (skia-canvas PNG filters 'auto', JPEG downsample), and outputs differ in size (Path2D PNG 331 KB vs 506 KB). Counter-evidence: the @napi-rs/canvas README tinybench run (benchmark/house.ts and gradient.ts, Apple M3 Max, an older skia-canvas, toBufferSync PNG export of a nearly blank 1024x768 canvas) has skia-canvas slower than node-canvas: 47 vs 60 ops/s and 46 vs 56 ops/s. The tested version is 4.0.0-rc6; the repo head is version 4.0.0-rc8 and CHANGELOG.md lists v4.0.0 dated Oct 1, 2026.

corrections.caveats: Snippet only: sixlabors.com is blocked here, so the 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 release-post numbers come from WebSearch result text, not an opened page; this verifier's snippets confirmed SkiaSharp 103.4 ms, CPU 43.0 ms, CPU retained 11.9 ms (3.1.0, up from 48.5 ms and 17.9 ms in 3.0) and WebGPU retained 5.476 ms (3.0.0), but not the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 / Windows 11 machine. Vendor posts, so first-party. Not like-for-like: FillParis.cs draws into a single-threaded SkiaSharp CPU raster SKSurface, while ImageSharp.Drawing's CPU backend builds the scene in parallel partitions and executes 16-pixel row bands with Parallel.For on all cores (src/ImageSharp.Drawing/Processing/Backends/DEFAULT_DRAWING_BACKEND.md; the benchmark's Setup raises the thread-pool minimum to Environment.ProcessorCount), so the 2.4x CPU win is many threads against one and likely slower per core; the retained-scene rows reuse geometry flattened and binned once in GlobalSetup while SkiaSharp redraws every SKPath each iteration; the WebGPU rows are GPU against Skia's CPU raster path (whether canvas.Flush() waits for GPU completion was not checked). Antialiasing is on for Skia (IsAntialias=true) and per-path transforms are pre-applied for every backend in SvgBenchmarkHelper, so the drawn work otherwise matches. The path-count wording differs between the code comment (30k) and the post (50K). C# (.NET) library, not callable from C++. Six Labors Split License 1.0 is not an OSI license for all users (Apache-2.0 only for open-source or source-available software, transitive dependencies, non-profits and companies under 1M USD annual revenue; paid commercial license otherwise), so usability is reference.
